tweets.text:
David Friedberg: Rising Rates Could Trigger a Banking Shock Right Before the Midterms

@friedberg:

“We've got a rate problem.

In the last 30 days or so, right, we've seen short-term rates on treasuries climb by 60 basis points.

And so this massive increase in rates is obviously going to impact people's ability to refinance their home, buy a new car, purchase things on credit, and the majority of Americans fall under that umbrella.

And I think there's also kind of an economic challenge ahead with the rate problem, and I would argue, as I always do, that the rate problem is fundamentally rooted in the federal government and the insane spending.

And if you look at the impact that this rate is gonna have on banks, there's 4295 banks that have positive equity that report FDIC, their balance sheets every month.

Based on the actual reported balance sheet of these banks, about 95 banks are going to see an impairment of more than 20% of their equity in the last 30 days or so.

And those reports start to come out on October 30th. So the thing I worry a lot about is on October 30th, we're going to kind of see all these financial reports coming out from all the banks, all the lending institutions, and there's about 95 of them that are going to say, ‘Hey, we've got more than 20% impairment charge on our equity.’

That's going to be a massive shock, and then what are the implications of that?

And that's where we're going to start to wake up to the fact that the rate problem isn't just a purchasing problem for consumers, but it may actually have a bit of a rippling effect here in the economy, starting with the financial institutions.

So they publish their next monthly reports on the September 30th ending period on October 30th, and unfortunately, it coincides right with the election cycle.”

tweets.text:
My best explanation of the “software factory” is to literally think about engineering output as a factory.

Before AI, software was mostly craftsmanship. The craftsmen were software engineers, and we spent decades optimizing everything around them: PMs writing specs so engineers worked on the right thing, better tooling, CI/CD, testing, infra, etc. But ultimately the throughput of the factory was still constrained by how much software humans could physically write.

Then the first wave of AI made the craftsmen much faster. Autocomplete, Cursor-style coding, pair programming with AI.

Now agents can increasingly take a feature end to end: understand the spec, inspect the codebase, write the code, test it, fix it, ship it. So for roughly the same human input, the output of the software factory starts going up dramatically.

And I think the end state people are chasing is a mostly autonomous software factory. Engineers write a spec / markdown file, define the tests and constraints, and become much more like verification engineers, while swarms of agents run 24/7 looking at telemetry, customer bugs, regressions, feature requests, then designing, coding, testing and shipping software.

But for that to actually work, the rest of the factory has to be insanely good too: CI/CD, tests, fast deployments, observability, security, rollback, evals, all of it.

It’s basically going from Ferrari building cars with incredible craftsmen doing a huge amount by hand, to the most advanced Tesla-style factory where more and more of the production line is automated.

And the big assumption behind all of this is that your product will eventually be as good as your software factory. If your factory is better, your agents can iterate faster, learn faster, ship more, and ultimately just build a better product.
